metaDescription: Five 4-1/2 inch angle grinders under $50 compared on amps, RPM, guard and switch, with the safety trade-offs a budget grinder makes and how to manage them.
expertTake: The Makita 9557PB is the best grinder you can find near this price: a 7.5-amp motor, a slim 2-1/2 inch barrel and a sealed gear drive from a brand that stocks parts. The WEN 944 at 7 amps and the DCA at 7.2 amps are the strong value picks, and the Metabo HPT kit is the one to choose if you want wheels and a case in the box. The SHALL at 4 amps is for light cutting only. Buy a flap disc and a face shield with any of them, because the wheel is where grinder safety lives.
introParagraphs: An angle grinder is a small, high-speed motor that spins an abrasive wheel at about 11,000 RPM, which cuts metal, grinds welds, strips rust and shapes masonry. It is the most versatile hand tool in a garage, and also one of the most dangerous, because the wheel is brittle and the speed is high.
This guide explains how motor rating, guard and switch design decide the safety and capability of a low-priced grinder, which compromises are fine for a homeowner and which are not.

products.name: Makita 9557PB 7.5-Amp 4-1/2 in Paddle Switch Angle Grinder
products.description:
The Makita 9557PB is the grinder most small shops buy first. A 7.5-amp motor spins at 11,000 RPM, and the barrel is only 2-1/2 inches in diameter, so a normal hand wraps around it. A paddle switch must be held to run, which means the grinder stops when you let go, and that is a basic safety feature that cheaper slide-switch grinders skip.

Makita uses labyrinth construction to seal the drive gear and bearings against dust, and metal grinding dust is the thing that kills cheap grinders. Compared with the WEN 944, which has a similar 7 amps, the Makita is smaller and better sealed. Against the SHALL at 4 amps, it has nearly twice the motor current, so it cuts and grinds without bogging.

Ownership notes: replace the stock wheel with a flap disc for general work, and always use the guard. The brushes are replaceable, and Makita stocks parts. If you want one grinder that you will still own in ten years, this is it. If you cut a lot of steel, a thin 1/16 inch cutting disc wastes less metal than a thick grinding wheel and throws fewer sparks into your face.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who want one grinder for metal, rust and tile with a safe switch.

products.name: WEN 944 7-Amp 4-1/2 in Angle Grinder with Reversible Handle
products.description:
The WEN 944 is a 7-amp grinder with an 11,000 RPM top speed, a reversible side handle and an arbor adapter that takes wheels with both 5/8 and 7/8-inch arbors. A reversible handle lets you mount it on either side for left-handed work, and a rubber grip lining reduces vibration.

Compared with the Makita 9557PB, the WEN has a nearly identical motor rating at a lower cost, but its housing is larger and its gear seal is simpler. Next to the DCA at 7.2 amps, it is almost interchangeable. What you gain is a known brand with a long track record in budget tools.

Ownership notes: check the guard before every use and tighten the wheel nut with the supplied wrench, not by hand. A grinder with a slide switch can run away if dropped, so keep both hands on it. For household grinding and cutting, it is a strong value. The handle can be threaded into three positions on most grinders, so mount it on the side that keeps your hand behind the wheel's plane of rotation.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a strong 7-amp grinder at a low outlay.
pros: Arbor adapter fits 5/8 and 7/8 in wheels
cons: Housing is larger than the Makita's
Slide switch can run away if dropped

products.name: DCA 7.2-Amp 4-1/2 in Corded Angle Grinder
products.description:
The DCA is a 7.2-amp, 860-watt grinder that spins up to 11,800 RPM. The maker lists a 7-inch grip circumference, which is slim, and a low-profile aluminum gear head that reaches into tight spots. Two safety guards ship in the box, which means you can use the grinder for cutting or grinding with the correct guard.

A higher top speed is not an advantage on its own. Abrasive wheels have a maximum rated RPM, and many 4-1/2 inch wheels are rated at 13,300, so 11,800 is within limits. Compared with the WEN 944 at 11,000, it spins about 7 percent faster.

For ownership, check that the wheel's rated RPM is above the tool's, tighten the nut firmly and use the correct guard for the task. A lesser-known brand means thin parts support. If you want the slimmest grip and a second guard at a low outlay, this is the pick. A slim grip also means the grinder is easier to keep steady against a vertical weld, which reduces the chatter that makes grinding marks.
products.bestFor: People with smaller hands who want a slim grinder with two guards.
pros: Aluminum gear head reaches tight spots

products.name: Metabo HPT 4-1/2 in 6.2-Amp Angle Grinder with Wheels and Case
products.description:
The Metabo HPT is a 6.2-amp grinder with a stated 980 watts of maximum output power, and it ships with five grinding wheels and a hard case. Metabo HPT is a major brand, formerly Hitachi, with a service network and parts. A spindle lock locks the spindle so you change wheels with a single wrench.

At 6.2 amps it has less motor current than the 7-amp WEN and DCA, but it is a better-built tool with a known name. The five wheels give you a starting supply. Compared with the Makita, the Metabo is a kit with a case, and the Makita is the tool with the sealed gear.

Ownership notes: keep the case dry so it protects the grinder from dust and moisture. Use the guard and store the wheels flat. If you want a name brand, a case and wheels in one box, this is the kit. The hard case matters more than it looks, because a grinder left loose in a toolbox picks up metal dust that works into the switch.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a major brand, a case and wheels in a single kit.
pros: Five wheels and a hard case included
Spindle lock for easy wheel changes
cons: 6.2 amps is less than the 7-amp picks

products.name: SHALL 4-1/2 in 4-Amp Angle Grinder with Guards and Discs
products.description:
The SHALL is the lightest and least powerful grinder here: a 4-amp, 500-watt motor, a weight of 3.7 pounds, and a package that includes two wheel guards, three cutting discs and three grinding wheels. It is a starter kit that lets you start cutting and grinding on day one.

At 4 amps it has about half the current of the Makita, so it slows in a heavy grind and heats under load. It is a tool for light cutting, thin metal and occasional jobs. Compared with the Metabo HPT at 6.2 amps, it is weaker, but it is lighter.

Ownership notes: do not lean on a small motor, let the wheel do the cutting and rest the tool when it heats. The included discs are basic, so upgrade them. For occasional use, it works, and for regular use, buy a 7-amp grinder. On thin sheet metal a 4-amp tool is fine, and cutting a 1/4 inch bolt takes a patient hand and a fresh disc.
products.bestFor: Occasional users who need to cut a bolt or grind a weld a few times a year.
cons: 4 amps is underpowered for heavy grinding

buyingCriteria.explanation: Grinders pull 4 to 10 amps at this price. A 7-amp motor, like the Makita and WEN, keeps its speed in a heavy grind. A 4-amp motor, like the SHALL, slows and overheats under the same load. The extra current buys you the ability to lean less. Think about what you will actually do: rust removal and paint stripping barely load a motor, while cutting 1/2 inch rebar or grinding down a thick weld load it hard and expose a weak tool. Brushes in a corded grinder also wear faster when the motor is overworked.

A paddle switch must be held to run, so it stops when you release it. A slide switch locks on, which is convenient and dangerous, because a dropped grinder keeps spinning. The Makita is paddle, and many budget grinders are slide. A lock-off is another safeguard. The extra step is to learn what the tool does if you drop it. A paddle grinder stops, and a lock-on slide grinder keeps spinning across the floor, which is why many shops forbid slide-switch grinders for overhead work.

Every abrasive wheel has a maximum RPM printed on it. The grinder's no-load speed must be at or below that rating. A 11,800 RPM grinder like the DCA needs wheels rated above that. Never use a wheel rated below the tool. Check the printed rating on the wheel itself rather than the box, and do not use a wheel with visible cracks, a dent or a wet storage history, since moisture weakens resin-bonded wheels.

The guard is the thing between you and the wheel if it shatters. Use the right guard for the task, and never remove it. A side handle adds control. Reversible handles, as on the WEN, suit left-handed users. Wear a face shield over safety glasses, not instead of them, plus hearing protection and gloves. A guard faces the user, and rotating it to the wrong position leaves you exposed.

A 2-1/2 inch barrel, as on the Makita, fits the hand and reduces fatigue. A heavy or fat grinder tires you out. Hold the tool before you buy if you can. Weight in the hand is not the same as spec-sheet weight, because a longer motor and a thick side handle change the balance. The 3.7 pound SHALL feels nimble, and a heavier 7-amp grinder is steadier on a long grind.

Metal dust is conductive and abrasive. A sealed gear head, like the Makita's labyrinth construction, extends life. Cheap grinders fail in a year of heavy grinding. After grinding steel, blow out the motor vents with compressed air, since metal dust that gets inside can arc across the windings and ruin the tool long before the brushes wear.

specDecoder.watchFor: Wheels have a maximum RPM, and the tool must not exceed it.

specDecoder.meaning: Current drawn at full load. 860 W at 120 V is about 7.2 amps.
specDecoder.watchFor: Peak watts on lesser brands can be inflated.

specDecoder.meaning: A switch you must hold to run.
specDecoder.watchFor: It is safer than a slide switch that locks on.

specDecoder.meaning: An abrasive disc made of overlapping sanding flaps.
specDecoder.watchFor: It is smoother and safer than a thick grinding wheel for general work.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared amps and RPM, from the SHALL's 4 amps to the Makita's 7.5 amps. We also considered brush access and cord length, since a short cord on a grinder drags across the work and gets nicked by sparks.

howWeEvaluated.title: Switch and safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We valued paddle switches, lock-off features and guards, because those decide how a grinder behaves when something goes wrong. A paddle switch and a lock-off button counted for more than any extra horsepower, because the safest budget grinder is one that stops when you let go.

howWeEvaluated.title: Build and sealing
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at gear head construction and dust sealing, noting the Makita's labyrinth design. We noted that sealed gear housings and aluminum gear heads cope better with metal dust than plastic housings.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit contents
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted guards, wheels and cases, noting the Metabo HPT's five wheels and hard case. We counted only the accessories that a buyer would actually use on day one, such as a second guard and cutting discs, and not the number of pieces in a bundle.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit for the cap
howWeEvaluated.description: Every grinder has a live price at or below the cap. We ranked each by how much safe cutting capacity a homeowner gets for the money.

howToChoose.intro: A grinder does three jobs, and each one wants a different disc and a different amount of motor.
These five grinders run from a light 4-amp tool to a 7.5-amp workhorse, and the ranking below follows motor current and build quality.

cards.label: Paddle
cards.text: Stops when released, so a dropped grinder stops. The Makita has one.

cards.label: Slide
cards.text: Locks on for continuous use, but a dropped grinder keeps spinning. The WEN and others use slide switches.

howToChoose.note: Choose a paddle switch for safety, and a slide for long grinding.

howToChoose.intro: Weight and slimness matter more than horsepower when you work overhead or on a vertical weld.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A thin cutting disc, a cutting guard and a firm grip. Clamp the work and let the disc do the cutting.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Makita and WEN have the power to cut bolts, and the DCA ships with two guards. The SHALL is limited to thin stock.

howToChoose.intro: Cutting metal puts the most strain on a small motor and on you, so the guard and disc matter more than the tool.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You grind daily or need a brushless cordless tool. A premium grinder lasts longer.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You use a grinder a few times a year. The WEN or SHALL is enough.

maintenance.why: A missing guard is the main cause of injuries.
A cut cord is a shock hazard.

faq.a: They can be, with a guard, a face shield and a properly rated wheel. Never remove the guard. A budget grinder is as safe as the wheel and guard on it, so replace the wheel with a rated flap disc and keep the guard in place.
It is the wheel diameter. It is the most common size. A 4-1/2 inch wheel is rated for roughly 13,300 RPM, which is why a grinder at 11,000 to 11,800 RPM is within its limits.
A flap disc for grinding and finishing, and a thin cutting disc for cutting. For rust and paint, use a flap disc with 60 to 80 grit, and for cutting rebar or bolts, use a thin reinforced cutoff disc.
A sudden jump when the wheel binds. A side handle and steady grip prevent it.

faq.q: Do I need a paddle switch?
faq.a: It is safer. If you buy a slide switch, keep both hands on the tool.

faq.q: Can I cut tile with a grinder?
faq.a: With a diamond blade, yes. Wear a mask.
